The first time I played this game, I couldn't stop thinking about it for weeks afterwards. I actually felt a bit traumatised. Not because this is by far the most gruesome game I have ever played (which it is), but because it contains themes that are difficult to digest like child abuse and child suicide. To me, this is far more disturbing than any of the visceral content of the game.

Needless to say, this is not a game for everyone, but then if you are playing this because you want to be scared out of your wits (and seriously, what other reason would you have to play this game?), prepare to be very satisfied.

The level design is a little bit less intuitive than Outlast, so if you stumble around, not entirely sure where to go next, prepare to die. A lot. As a result, the fear aspect of the game suffers a bit, because the point in being scared is really in trying to AVOID death, rather than actually dying until it becomes trial and error. However, maybe that's just me. Doubtless other gamers will navigate the game far better than I did.

Like its predecessor, Outlast 2 gives the player no weapons and the only way to avoid danger is to run and hide. A formula that continues to work brilliantly and terrifyingly.

All in all, I love this game. If you've got a strong stomach, you might too.

Being a huge fan of the first Outlast, I really wanted to love this game. Unfortunately, it seems to have missed (or simply eschewed) a lot of what worked so well in the first game. The shift from claustrophobic hallways to open forest means environments are harder to visually parse and navigate, which I assume the developers intended to evoke dread and hopelessless, but generally is just confusing and frustrating. The first game favored areas that allowed for running away, hiding, and regrouping. In this game, many sections fall victim to trial-and-error with a likelihood of repeated deaths that feel more like poorly put together puzzles. Sadly, repetition is not scary. Being lost is not scary. Similarly, the game regularly breaks its own momentum with sequences that interrupt gameplay and psychological pacing.

The story is engaging enough, and I appreciated the effort to package it a little differently than Outlast 1 and to avoid repeating what many considered a weak ending, but I think the overall effect is more extravagent but less cohesive and enganging for the player.

All that said, the game looks great and has some genuinely interesting and enjoyable moments. I don't regret buying it or playing it, but I did find it inferior to the first game.

TL:DR: If you liked the first outlast for it's stealth sections this game probably isn't for you. Too much running around.

I'll start by mentioning what is good about this game and then delve into the reason why I would not recommend it.
This game is absolutely beautiful with an interesting soundtrack and amazing attention to detail. They did an amazing job when setting this game up to be a proper successor to the first Outlast game. From the moment you start playing the atmosphere hits you upside the head from the subtle music queues to the dreary setting, everything is perfectly in place to make you feel that excellent sense of dread.


Unfortunately I didn't get this feeling from this game. Where the first Outlast game had a constant sense of nervousness and uncertainty, this game replaces with mainly frustration. Your sense of fear and dread fades early on and if you're anything like me you'll get annoyed fast. There was a much larger emphasis placed on stealth in the first game and although there were some improvements made to the stealth system in Outlast 2 there were far too many scripted events where your character gets discovered and you have to run. This is also combined with unclear paths or small exits that are easy to miss, so I got frustrated easily while playing this game and never actually got to finish it. There is so much running in this game that I often just stopped playing because I was feeling physically tired because it would sometimes take me 15 minutes to find the one small window that I needed to jump through or crawl under. Unfortunately as a player and in real life too I'm not good at looking for things unless I at least have an idea of what I'm looking for so there were some points where I wasn't able to progress unless I looked up a playthrough to find the small hole in the corner of the screen that I had to find while being chased by an incredibly fast enemy or a horde of incredibly slow enemies.

This issue with the running around may not sound like much but in a horror game building up your atmosphere is key to that psychological horror that this series is known for. If you spend 60% of your time running in circles that initial adrenaline from getting discovered falls hard and your body responds as such by getting tired and you, the player, feeling apathetic. In a good horror game you're normally catching your breath at times like these but in this game I would stop getting scared and just be running at this point so I was tired, not scared, and still running; I couldn't find whatever exit I was looking for and getting very annoyed. The reason the first Outlast succeeds where this one fails is the sequences where you have to run are organically created. The player may fail and get spotted by an enemy which will prompt them to run. The fear that has been building up releases at this point as the music picks up which causes the player to get more frightened and leads to a short chase sequence where the player either gets away or dies, both resulting in the player getting to catch their breath and think about their situation.

Take Alien Isolation as another example. The player has to get out of a situation that is unwinnable. You're sneaking around a ship with a killer alien on board. If you don't hide well, you die hard. The best horror game doesn't just create an atmosphere. It creates an environment where the player works themselves up. When a horror game is set up well the player will be the one causing themselves the most fear.

I would not recommend this game if you liked the first Outlast, but if you like running A LOT then this game should be fine for you.

I was REALLY excited to play this game when it was done downloading. I'm a huge fan of Outlast 1 and horror games in general so I was looking forward to getting the shit scared out of me. I was disappointed with the final product and I've made some semi-coherent points about why it didn't succeed as well as it could have.

Very mild spoilers ahead - nothing that will ruin the game for you.

The enemies are much smarter than in the previous game, so much so that they're borderline psychic. This seems great at first, but eventually makes the game feel a bit rigged. I played on Normal mode and it felt like the enemies were jacked up in difficulty. I'd get seen by an enemy, I'd run into a basement and hide. He'd investigate to see where I am, I'd hide, he'd leave, and then as I try to leave again he'd see me with his flashlight and come back, forcing me to wait again. Rinse and repeat.

The game doesn't reward stealth gameplay. I've watched LetsPlays of people who just charge through and have much better results than me: someone who's trying to exercise caution in a village surrounded by psychopaths that frequently make a beeline for the player before killing them in a corner.

I remember in the first game there was a really great scripted chase sequence that leads to you meeting Dr. Trager, a really great character. I hope you liked that scripted chase sequence because there are about 20 of them SHOVED in your face by the end of the game and it loses its appeal incredibly quickly.

I was hoping for more stealth gameplay, since the moments in the game where you hide and hope an enemy goes away were VERY scary. A great gameplay mechanic is when you have to hide in a barrel - you can kind of see through some holes in the metal and if you pop up to get a clear look you risk being seen. Same with water and water-filled barrels - you need to surface to avoid drowning so there's this great tension of "I'll die if I don't look but I might get caught if I do, so I'm just gonna risk it and look." Once time I did this and an enemy was directly in front of me with his back turned - a *really* close call.

But the thing about stealth that's so much scarier than running from a pre-determined chase sequence is this: when I'm sneaking around enemies, it's scary knowing I could get caught and killed; the scary music will come back, the enemy will continue hitting me and obscuring my vision, and it generally won't be fun.

When the game throws you into a bunch of enemies screaming at you while you run away, the worst has happened; you've been caught, now you have to run and try to survive. The tension has been removed, it's just chaos and loud noises. There's no subtlety. It would be much scarier if, after a chase sequence, instead of the music vanishing and the game saying "k you're safe," if you had to lay low for a minute or two while the enemy loses sight of you and then wanders off- that would be much less mechanical and abrupt than just sequeing into normal gameplay again.

When you're forced to run from something and you don't have the option to hide, you become aware of "okay I'm currently being chased," and as soon as you run into a cave and the rocks crumble behind you, thereby ending the chase, you think "okay I'm no longer being chased." There's no sense of relief that comes from losing your pursuers because you know there's just going to be another scripted chase scene around the corner.

One thing I REALLY like is the ability to lock doors behind you, and it's funny to imagine the enemies in Outlast 1 were so stupid that they had to ram down an unlocked door. If you forget to lock them, enemies will just open the door without thinking about it, and if you close a door behind you as you're being pursued, you'll freak out a little bit as you try to deadbolt the door before the enemy beats you to the punch. There's a bit in which you're trying to sneak past a big brute: normally enemies will ram a door 3-5 times before the lock breaks, but this dude rams the door ONCE and crushes it open, which really freaked me out as I realized this guy was seriously going to destroy me if he got close.

Another cool detail is that enemies can now pursue you in a variety of ways. In Outlast 1, once you jumped across a ledge or crawled under an obstacle you knew the enemy wouldn't be able to follow you, likely because the game's AI wasn't developed-enough to handle it - you knew you were safe because the enemies were stupid. In this game, enemies can crawl after you, which may not be a massive deal, but that feeling of "oh this guy can't get me because I crawled through this hole" is shattered once you realize the enemies have gotten a lot smarter and will follow you extensively in order to kill you.

The worst part of the game is these weird flashback/hallucinations about your old Catholic middle school and your high school friend named Jessica being dead. There's a lot of forced images of Jessica hanging from a noose - the only documents you see throughout these dream sections are some papers with the "Hangman" game drawn on them. Ominous phrases like "I'll never let you go" and "Jessica Loves Blake" will be thrown in there with seemingly no relevance to the story. Eventually the dream sequences get a monster that chases you in a straight line and then despawns once you get far enough or open a door, which was definitely an improvement, but nothing ruined my fun more than opening a door and seeing the game transition into the school hallways, knowing I was about to be bored and confused.

The problem with these segments is that they occur WAY too frequently. I want to say they happen roughly 12 times throughout the game, maybe as an attempt to compensate for the intense pace of the chase sequences by offering what the game developers thought was "a creepy, slow-paced atmosphere." If that isn't enough, the dreams regularly show a creepy priest following around Jessica. Anyone with a brain knows that a Catholic priest being creepy around children has a very strong implication behind it, but then as the game is wrapping up they basically shove it in your face that the priest did something to Jessica - Red Barrels thought they were being SUBTLE when a little girl was screaming for help while a priest chased her through the school hallways, but then at the end they use a cutscene to say "Yes this is indeed what happened, just in case you were wondering."

The antagonists weren't even interesting - there are two sides known as the Christians and the Heretics. There's Knoth, a morbidly obese prophet and the primary angagonist of the game, a woman carrying a pickaxe who chases you throughout the game muttering Bible quotes, a big ogre carring a dwarf on his back who shoots flaming arrows at you, and a creepy woman who leads the Heretics that chases you in the mines. Aside from that there's just you and your wife Lynn, who's your primary incentive to push forward, and by the end very few questions are answered. You don't read any documents that give you cool backstory to the enemies, building them up before you actually meet them face to face. 

The story is very mediocre. The only time I was excited to see characters talking with me was the hope that they'd add some variety to the game and maybe give me some context as to what I'm doing or where I'm going, but by the end of the game every interesting question of "Who is this character?" and "Why do they want to kill children?" is swept under the rug with the general answer of "Religion is evil lol."

I'd say this game is passable, but it would be much better at 20 dollars rather than 30. The main problem is that it isn't as scary as Outlast and it tries way too hard to freak players out, much to the detriment of the final product. It's a fine game, just don't expect it to be as good as the first one and/or its DLC.

That was intense. This diabolical chase simulator doesn't dwell on the more stealthy approach of the original. Instead, you can deal with the enemy encounters mostly through trial and error/death and running a lot. You'll have a lot of reasons for running, as you barely escape rednecks with machetes, an eerie grim reaper figure, heretics, zealots and their religious leader Papa Sullivan Knoth. 

Where the game excels is not in the fanatical hick town, but in the atmospheric flashbacks of your school days in a Catholic school. Empty hallways, total silence and deadly jumpscares (I screamed a little, which doesn't happen very often to me). As you progress, you'll slowly uncover the fate of your classmate, while being spooked and of course chased by some twisted, perverse demon with a lot of hands and a long tongue. The flashbacks alternate with your real-world situation and create a nice dynamic.

Even though the gameplay is about running and occasionally hiding, the lack of any means of offense is bafflingly absurd. Yes, you can sometimes break free from the clutches of your adversaries by doing a quick-time event, but getting caught usually means death and restart from checkpoint. There are makeshift weapons lying all around, but the main character focuses solely on his camera and running skills. The camera is now full HD and has a new microphone function that lets you approximate enemy movement and sound through walls and long distances. You can hide in barrels, closets or under beds, but you will almost always get caught because the enemies can detect you very easily.

The change of environment from Mount Massive Asylum's hallways to an Arizona desert is mainly visual because both locations are presented in a linear fashion. There are no alternate routes and the sprawling town of Temple Gate seems very small from your perspective.

The story is well-done, speaks mainly about religious themes in incomprehensible mumbo-jumbo and has a strong albeit cliffhanger finale. It isn't well-defined as there are many possible interpretations of what has transpired in the game and the intense ending.

The game is surprisingly advanced (considering the small indie team) in terms of graphics and attention to detail. The character models are on a par with AAA games. The engine is well-optimized.

I am a bit biased toward horror games, but all in all, it was a memorable experience and I would recommend it to anyone looking for some adrenaline and spookiness. And a lot of gore and shock value moments. Knowledge of the original is not required. The third game has been announced.

7.5/10

+ strong atmosphere (especially in the school), fluid alternation of real-world situations with traumatic flashbacks, detailed graphics, shock value events and story
- the gameplay is not that elaborate, chase simulator, death-fest, enemy AI seems like cheating

After waiting a long time for Outlast 2, being a fan of the first one, I still don't know exactly what happend here. It pains me to say that it feels like a pretty mediocre horror title. It relies too much on a heavy ambience that never really gets to be scary, and the gameplay and level design makes it all completely fall apart. It's almost as if it was made by a completely different studio that wanted to make a copycat but never understood what makes the first game great.

The story starts pretty good, and after a very interesting introduction of a few antagonists and their motivations, it stops in its tracks, and it never gets past that. The game feels like a huge wasted potential, where nothing really happens. Only the levels change, as the story comes to a halt, throwing some new characters around, and making them appear again, but just like they were at the start, with no development. It's not that the plot is uninspired, as it's completely lacking. Everything seems to be there to make it great, but they only seem to be concerned with a very broken gameplay. The devs say that the we can only understand the story deeply by reading all the hidden logs scattered around and, I'm sorry, but if you need to piece together almost all of the story through collectible hidden items, there's something really wrong with your script. Also, the documents, as fun as they may be to read, are pretty shallow, and only manage to throw around some superficial ideas tied to the plot.

If I had to say one word that describes Outlast 2 gameplay, it would be Inconsistent. They break their own rules constantly, and that's what completely kills the game in my opinion. Already in the first hostile encounter you're supposed to understand that you can't run faster than them, and you can't sneak around since they will always detect you. Instead, you'll have to make it follow you, to despawn after you run back for a while, so you can continue. That would be kind of a spoiler, if there ever was any explanation for that in game. As it is, you just have to try it until, somehow, it works for you. After that first enemy, you'll never have to do that again. In other sections, you're supposed to guess if you have to get around the enemies to continue the path forward or run from them to find an alternate path, with absolutely no hint of where to go or what to do. This becomes pretty jarring on higher difficulties, specially on insane (permadeath difficulty), since it now seems most encounters are cheap or based on luck, and instead of being strategic, you now have to completely memorize the paths and understand exactly how the AI works. I finished Outlast 1 on insane difficulty and it was great, but I'll never try on this one.

Unlike the first Outlast, there's no indication to where you should go. Instead of the clever design of the lighting and colors to show you the way, you will find illuminated paths that go nowhere, and will be completely lost for a big part of the game, while having enemies constantly trying to kill you. The chase sequences are overused and terribly annoying because without some clues in the level telling you where to go, you'll have to die lots of times trying to find the exit. The game then loses it's - already pretty low - scare factor and becomes incredibly frustrating and tiresome. The trial and error that players keep reporting is real, and an annoyance instead of a challenge. Also gone are the neutral NPCs that looked exactly like the aggresive ones. It was a great detail for a horror game, adding tension to every contact with the asylum inmates, but now, there's no tension anymore, as you'll soon understand that any NPC will attack you mindlessly on sight even if they look passive enough.

The camera got an upgrade, but it's mostly to make it more frustrating. The added directional microphone can help, but it consumes so much battery that is almost unusable. You also need to keep the camera running and directed at the scenes for a few seconds to get the recordings, something that, in my opinion, really detracts from the gameplay - though it's a minor annoyance, not really a feature, as it was advertised. Since the game now has a lot of pitch black areas with no "guiding" light, nightvision is absolutely necessary. It would be a good thing if it wasn't for the scarcity of the batteries in higher difficulties, since you can be absolutely screwed on dark chase sequences, where you need to rely on your artificial light to find the right path.

There's also no sense of progression, as you keep going to completely different places that seem loosely connected and you'll never know if you're close to your objective. It doesn't help that you're shifting in and out of school levels that don't really add substantial story content - even though the transition sequences are pretty damn cool - as they're mostly about exploring - an admittedly beautifully rendered - school level until you somehow get out. The ambience is pretty well done, but it gets very boring as you keep revisiting it to find mostly the same narrative with almost no changes, until closer to the end.

The game has a few things that it does really well, like the great optimization and low recommended specs for such a beautiful title - some frame drops might happen, even for those with high end PCs, but it might be fixed in a future patch. The art design is probably the best I've seen on a game, and that says a lot for a horror themed one. This is my honest review of Outlast 2.

Listen—I love the game, and you might be asking, “If you love it, why are you giving it a mostly negative review?” The answer is simple: the game is WAY too drawn out.

The first Outlast perfected the formula—it was short, tight, and terrifying. Outlast 2, by contrast, is long, repetitive, and, at times, just plain boring. The biggest offender? The endless flashbacks to the high school. The first few were clever, but by the 15th time, it felt comically forced. It becomes less “psychological horror” and more “oh look, spooky guy—run again.” It stops being scary and starts being annoying.

Instead of feeling tense and sneaking through areas, I found myself just sprinting past everything to get it over with. The immersion breaks when the gameplay loop becomes so repetitive and predictable.

Truthfully, they could cut 60% of the walking simulator content and the game would still hit the same emotional and narrative beats—and honestly, it would be a much tighter experience if they did. If the devs make another game in this style (besides Outlast: Trials), I beg you: do not pack it with this much filler between actual plot points. It just becomes exhausting.

If you want to make a longer game, make it interesting—not just a repetitive cycle of wandering around and looting houses for batteries and bandages.

TL;DR Outlast 2 is an okay horror game, its longer but not as good as the original and its DLC. Level design is frustrating. Story is poorly told.

Outlast 2 is the second full-fledged instalment of the Outlast series, after the wild success of Outlast and it's DLC, titled "Whistleblower". The original Outlast introduced the hide-and-run mechanic alongside camcorder night-vision. The idea that you couldn't fight back against any of the threats in Mount Massive Asylum added to the terror, and these same mechanics make a return in the sequel.

In comparison to Outlast, Red Barrels had a much stronger budget with Outlast 2. This shows in multiple areas; the character you control, Blake, is actually voice acted. The environments are more diverse, the models and lighting are more impressive - including parts of the game where the player is transitioned into Blake's Catholic school. The game is longer, clocking in at roughly four hours - more if you want to get all collectibles. There are new mechanics that have been implemented such as bandages to heal yourself, a microphone option on your camcorder and the finite ability to sprint when chased.  It's clear that Red Barrels stuck to the original Outlast formula - why change what isn't broken? They kept the night-vision, the recording of events, the note finding, the intense chase moments, the occasionally puzzle solving, and the notorious antagonists. However, the execution in Outlast 2 is where things differ, and for the worse.

In Outlast, the environment is confined to an asylum, therefor corridors and rooms are common, and while it can be maze-like at times, its usually pretty straightforward where one needs to go to advance to the next area in the game. In Outlast 2, the environment takes place in a rural, mountainous region somewhere in the Arizona desert. The open, outside environments creates the first and largest problem with Outlast 2 - knowing where the f*ck to go most of the time.

The general formula to the Outlast games is getting spotted = RUN. 

This straightforward formula is ruined when, at times, it's unclear where to go. This problematic event happens at multiple parts in the game, in each chapter, even at the Catholic school flashbacks. The game switches from being terrifying to being frustrating. The player has too many "open areas" to navigate; cliffs, forests, lakes, full sized towns - even having to go underneath some houses and navigate through fields of corn. Even in its linear, closed off sections, such as the Catholic school, its a pain to know exactly where to go - often the correct path seems random or incredibly unclear. It's an indication of awful level design and Outlast 2 is full of it - which is really confusing as Outlast's level design was great and with such a smaller budget. Admittedly, I got stuck in Outlast also, but not due to the layout of the level but more because I was not familiar with the layout. Once I became familiar with the layout, I had the advantage in every chase scene. Replaying Outlast 2 to get the bonus achievements, I kept noticing that the path that leads to progression is so not obvious to a beginner player. And even having finished the game previously, I still managed to get stuck again.

The protagonist finds himself stuck (pun intended) in a valley full of religious psychotic people, with strange flashes of light coming from towers around the area. The townsfolk that you come across all seem to be going insane and are twisted by their faith, they kill and torture others, including the player, for some sort of religious incentive - whether its for sinning or the apocalypse. I'm not even sure as the story is kind of bland and at no point attempts to explain what the hell has happened to this region. Unfortunately, Red Barrels chose the cheapest and most piss-poor of all options when it comes to telling a game's narrative; confining all explanation to a single note collectible found next to a lake mid-game. I won't bother explaining as it will reveal some spoilers, but wow, talk about pathetic storytelling. And it's not even that obvious of a location, so the player can easily miss it on their first attempt through the game.

While Outlast was full of scares, it had almost a hilarious outrageous nature to its horror. Mount Massive Asylum was just too crazy to believe - and it totally worked for that game. In Outlast 2, it feels like everything is taken so much more seriously, amplified by the in-your-face message that "religion is BAAAD!!".

I mentioned earlier that Blake was voice-acted, which is unique compared to Outlast. At first, this definitely felt like a potential to add personality and connection the main character. However, all that this really resulted in was the protagonist spouting things like "F*ck! F*ck! F*ck!", and "Oh f*ck me! Oh f*ck this sh*t!", and "Gotta find Lynne, nothing else matters!". It's incredibly shallow to the point that, sadly, it wasn't even really necessary.

The antagonists in Outlast 2 (Marta, Val and Knoth)( do not measure up to the same reputation as their predecessors in Outlast (Trager, Eddie Gluskin and Chris Walker). [spoiler] Marta is essentially Outlast 2's Chris Walker - albeit her final scene was much less satisfying than Chris Walker's. I'm not even sure what happened to Val at the end of the game, and we interact with Knoth for about 5% of the whole game [/spoiler]

Despite all the negative sentiments I've laid out for Outlast 2, it does retain the horror element in spite of its flaws. The game's different environments are quite memorable, and the aforementioned parts of the game where we visit Blake's Catholic school are transitioned exceptionally well. The Catholic school sections are undoubtedly the most disturbing parts of the game, and really make me wish that Outlast 2 only took place inside the school. There are also sections where the school takes on a surreal form, amplifying the feeling of dread and the horror that took place here for the characters. 

The music, in my opinion, is much more experimental, whereas Outlast relied heavily on violins and orchestral instruments, Outlast 2 uses unconventional horror sounds using instruments such as banjos to fit the game's setting. The game's composer, Samuel Laflamme, is very talented as the game would lose about half of its fear factor if it weren't for the hear-pumping and bone chilling soundtrack.

Lastly, Outlast 2 is a good horror experience, but a huge step down from Outlast, when it should have been equally, if not better, than the original due to the company's increased budget. I suppose this is an example of how money doesn't automatically mean the end product will be better. I think Red Barrels became sidetracked with Outlast 2, and they forgot what made Outlast so special. I hope that Outlast 3, or whatever their future title is called, will retain more of the magic of the original game and sacrifice less for the purpose of making a larger game.

[h1]Mount Massive was a pebble in a pond, an experiment on individuals. This is where the real sickness spreads[/h1] 

[h1]Introduction[/h1] 
The original Outlast had a creepy atmosphere with terrifying enemies that chased you throughout the game. [b]Outlast 2[/b] not only improves on this concept, slightly, but gives us a horror experience, that is not filled with jump scares, while giving us a setting that I personally found better than the original’s. The AI. has also been improved, and will act differently than the ones in the first game. [b]Red Barrels[/b] have improved, on what they can offer, to make a unique and yet amazing horror experience. I should also give a warning to anyone that plays this game; there are scenes of extreme gore, this game is not recommended for the faint of heart, especially if you hate seeing bad things happen to children. 

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1] 
[b]Pros[/b] 
[list]
[*]The story has a really good setting inside a creepy town full of corrupt cultists 
[*]The AI. has been improved, while the horror has fewer jump scares
[*]Sound detectors were an interesting feature, that I really liked to use. 
[*]The graphics are well done and feel very creepy.

[/list]
[b]Cons[/b] 
[list] 
[*]The story suffers from bad writing.
[*]Sound detectors are underused. 
[*]The path throughout the game is linear; no twists or turns, with some hiding. 
[/list]

[h1]Story[/h1] 
[b]Blake Langermann[/b] is with his wife [b]Lynn,[/b] to investigate the murder of [b]Jane Doe.[/b] The two go on a chopper because the desert area is, for the most part, rocky and unpassable with a vehicle. When the two start to film the report, they see a white flash of light and it causes the chopper to break down and crash. When [b]Blake[/b] wakes up, he finds the pilot skinned, and his wife [b]Lynn[/b] missing. He then finds out that he is in a little town run by [b]Sullivan Knoth,[/b] who runs a corrupt religious cult, and thinks the End Times are upon them, with [b]Blake[/b] in the midst of it. 
 
The setting for [b]Outlast 2[/b] is its strong point; in the first game, we were put into an asylum that had crazy people all over the place. [b]Outlast 2[/b] not only improves on this concept but brings us something even more messed up than an overrun asylum. The creepy town looks and works nicely as you can sense the amount of dread, as things are not normal and anything can happen at any given moment. You are in a town out in the middle of nowhere, with no way to contact anyone, it may not look like much at first, but this kind of setting is what makes [b]Outlast 2[/b] shine. Also, [b]Blake’s[/b] glasses are made out of really durable steel as they don’t break on really high falls; same with his bones as they don't seem to break either.
 
Regardless of [b]Outlast 2's[/b] great setting, its writing is questionable at times. For example: [b]Blake[/b] walks towards a church for help early in the game, and yet his previous encounters with the town's inhabitants should be enough to ward him away from it.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1] 
[b]Outlast 2,[/b] in terms of gameplay, is very similar to the first one with adjustments to the AI.. You can’t attack or defend; you will be running from enemies as they chase you throughout the town and the only thing you can do is run and hide. The camcorder makes a return with a new HUD and sound detectors that you can use to find enemies [b]Blake[/b] can’t see with his eyes. You can use night vision to see in the dark. The night vision and the sound detectors do use batteries; playing on harder difficulties will make batteries scarcer and be consumed faster. There are a lot of areas that are lit up, so only use the night vision, when you really need it, and only switch batteries, when the camcorder is really low. The AI. has been improved from the first game and will act differently; the AI. will be more aggressive on higher difficulties and will look in hiding spots. If you play on easy, the enemies will be less aggressive, and some chase scenes will be removed. I played on hard as the mechanics are pretty much the same and nothing has really changed other than some minor tweaks. The horror has also been improved and is less focused on jump scares and more on the horror aspect itself, which is something that I liked as a whole. 
 
Now, the gameplay is nicely done as a whole, however, there are two issues that I found. [b]Outlast 2[/b] has a very liner path with some turns and hiding added. It’s not liked the original [b]Outlast[/b] where you had many ways to go around the enemies throughout. The sound detectors were a feature I loved but were underused; there were not a lot of moments where I found them to be useful and I really only used them in cornfields where I could not see the enemy.

[h1]Graphics and Performance[/h1] 
[b]Outlast 2[/b] runs on [b]Unreal Engine 3,[/b] the game looks really beautiful and creepy, each area felt unique to go through as well as feeling real in its own way. The game sounds creepy as well, hearing the villagers chant puts a feel of distress at times. I loved going through the town as it felt like a place you would see in the early 1600s and 1700s. I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, an AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and 16 GB of RAM storage. The game ran at 60 FPS and was smooth throughout my experience as I encountered no issues while playing. You will need a decent computer for it to run but the game is not too demanding.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1] 
[b]Outlast 2[/b] is a great sequel to the original. If you liked the first one, then you will most certainly like the second game. The game has a fantastic setting that I feel is a step up from a crazy asylum and it’s something that I truly loved. I had a really nice time with playing it and I felt scared on some of the chase scenes that were thrown at me.

I don't think I've ever been this conflicted about wether or not I liked a game. Maybe I should start off by saying, I don't usually play horror games. It's not my genre. I'm hard to scare, but easy to startle. 

Outlast 2 is, for the most part, extremely boring. For the majority of the game, you sneak around, using the tools at your disposal, nightvision and a directional microphone, to avoid enemies searching for you. Generally, the objective during these sections is simply to get from A to B, usually around an obstacle like a big enemy, a broken bridge, you name it. Then, after several sneaking sections, you get discovered by no fault of your own, then you're forced to run away on a straight path until you enter the next scripted cutscene. If you get discovered during the sneak sections, the enemies will chase you but are generally easy to shake by hiding in an obvious spot. You then return to sneaking with the only penalty being time lost.

Sometimes, the enemies just kill you. There are plenty enemies that can kill you in one hit. Either they bitchslap you and you pass out immediately, or you go into a gory death animation. After seeing this once, it really loses all its terror. Towards the end of the game, I found myself just sprinting through the areas, bumping into appearing enemies, dying and then running past those areas. You could consider this a form of "progression" where the pace picks up compared to the beginning, however I would not. The game was not designed for you to die repeatedly to discover enemy locations, then speedrun past them. If you played the game as intended, you'd be doing the exact same thing over and over. Enemies all work pretty much exactly the same with some minor gimmicks. 

Characters in this game... exist. They are memorable because of how grotesque they are, but for the most part nothing that's gonna pull in a cult following. The player character and his story is pretty fleshed out and definitely the strongest part of the game. However, the enemies just feel generic and never really all that terrifying. 

So if you can't scare the player with that, what do you do? You include extreme gore, disturbing imagery, scarce resources and high stakes. Outlast 2 is very hit and miss when it comes to this. There is a ton of gore, only very little of which really affected me. I feel like it's extremely exaggerated while taking itself too seriously, and what is there would have been a lot more effective if they hadn't held it in your face the entire time. A little restraint in the gore department would've made it a lot more believable and as such scarier.

All that considered, within the realm of "Helplessly sneaking around and running away" Horror games, Outlast still sets the gold standard. Sound design is top notch, graphics are beautiful and the visual design, scene composition, and the way they play with symbolism, surreal imagery and use light is very very good. The path forward is sometimes rather easy to miss but unlike other games, I only found myself stuck in an area with no obvious exit a select few times. It's frustrating if it happens, and you feel dumb when you realize what you should have been doing, but it's not really something that takes away from the game as a whole. 
The topics explored feel a bit generic but generally well executed and the story is engaging enough to keep you pushing through the game. Unlike the gameplay, if you look at the narrative, nothing outstays its welcome.

I'd give it a 6.5/10 - very solid game that shines in a select few areas - just nothing really groundbreaking or new, and with a pretty basic main gameplay loop that is only made bearable by how competently everything else is executed. Buy on sale.

I love horror games. Various Silent Hills, Resident Evils, Dead Spaces, Amnesias, Penumbras (one of them, anyway), Outlast 1 and the Whistleblower DLC, Dreadhalls, etc. I LOVE scary games.

This game, however, did not scare me at all.

That is overwhelmingly due to the fact that you are constantly being chased. CONSTANTLY. Run from enemies here, jump over a fence, come across new enemies 45 seconds later to run from, slide down a hill, come across new enemies 1 minute later that chase you through a house, underneath the floor boards, out in to a courtyard and through another house, back under the same floor boards but out a new exit this time, and down an elevator. Phew. 2 minutes later, the same enemies from 2 times ago chase you through yet another little village with a corn field this time (ooooh).

Honestly, it was so tedious and frustrating that I was beyond scaring. The best, most unnerving parts in the entire game were parts where you weren't actually in danger at all, simply because they FINALLY let the tension breathe! They finally gave the horror the room it needed to get in to your bones, and they finally started playing with your mind rather than having you once again sprint from samey-enemy #47. There's a reason that so many good horror movies follow the "the less you see, the better" trope.

The developers spent so much time creating this astoundingly-beautiful world and filling it with horrific elements and seriously disturbing imagery, and then had you spend all your time running through it, pursued by the same 5 enemies!

Another frustrating element to this is the fact that they severely dialed up the threat the enemies pose. I'm not talking about how the enemies kill you if they catch you, I'm talking about how the enemies seem to know exactly where you are at all times. I get that a lot of it is scripted, but when an enemy slinks out of the shadows 300 feet ahead of me, and I back away from the corner I was barely peeking out of to hide in an unseen barrel, the enemy should not be able to bee-line directly to the exact barrel I'm hiding in (which they never saw), and pull me out. Having to replay sections in a horror game absolutely kills the tension, and having to repeat the same section 8 times trying to find the one specific thing I'm supposed to do in order to advance to the next chase sequence is just maddening. The best moments in horror games (and moments that other games like Amnesia and the first Outlast got so right) were moments where an enemy popped out of a corner, so you turn around and book it, making a mad scramble to get away, which you do by the skin of your teeth.

I never got that feeling from this game. I either did it the exact pixel-perfect way the developers intended every single time, or I failed, every single time. I'm playing a horror game, not memorizing boss patterns in Mega Man! [h1] Outlast 2 - A Gritty Descent into Darkness [/h1]

In the realm of horror gaming, "Outlast 2" takes a unique and unrelenting approach. It doesn't just want to scare you; it aims to terrify you, immersing you in a nightmarish world of fear, confinement, and relentless dread.

The game frequently deploys a shocking narrative principle - let's call it "Chekhov's piss." If you witness something repulsive, like a mutant hillbilly urinating among decapitated heads and severed body parts, brace yourself to crawl through that filth in the next 15 minutes or so. This game doesn't pull punches or rely on subtle implications. It's a brutal exercise in terror and cruelty, forcing you to endure horrifying scenarios in excruciating detail.

Developed and published by Red Barrels, "Outlast 2" embraces a direct approach to terror. Its eagerness to make players squirm, confronting them with gruesome and disturbing imagery, is both impressive and unsettling. However, this directness sometimes lacks a clear narrative purpose. "Outlast 2" knows it wants to shock you but struggles to convey a cohesive message.

[u] [b] Setting the Stage:  [/b] [/u]

Before delving deeper, it's crucial to note that "Outlast 2" tackles extremely heavy and uncomfortable topics, often without much tact or delicacy. Themes of religion, body horror, misogyny, and sexual abuse are pervasive, and the game doesn't shy away from graphic and explicit content. If this doesn't align with your preferences, it's best to steer clear.

You assume the role of Blake, a mild-mannered videographer, and alongside your reporter wife, Lynn, you're investigating the mysterious death of a pregnant 15-year-old girl named Jane Doe. She was found wandering a desolate highway miles from civilization, with ties to Temple's Gate, a secluded religious community hidden in the mountains. Your helicopter crashes during filming, separating you from Lynn and plunging you into a nightmare.

Alone and armed only with your camera's night vision and directional microphone, you explore the cult's eerie compound. Even before you encounter knife-wielding cultists, unsettling piles of child corpses, and cryptic notes about apocalypse and monstrous sun creatures, it's evident you're in a dire situation.

[u] [b] The Power of the Camera: [/b] [/u]
The game's camera mechanic isn't just a gimmick to ride the found-footage horror trend or provide night vision and eerie whispers caught on the directional microphone. It's a tool that makes you linger on the horrors you encounter. You're compelled to record gruesome scenes and document cryptic passages from the cult's bizarre gospel. You're not there to intervene; you're there to witness and record the horror, a duty that becomes your burden.

This integration of gameplay mechanics with narrative themes is well-executed, but unfortunately, the game's overall narrative doesn't achieve the same level of cohesion.

[u] [b] Lost in Ambiguity: [/b] [/u]

While the original "Outlast" and its expansion, "The Whistleblower," effectively forced players to confront uncomfortable ideas, their criticisms and themes were more apparent and coherent. "Outlast 1" offered a clear commentary on the cruelty of the military-industrial complex, connecting the Mount Massive Asylum's horrors to the real-life MKUltra program's debauchery.

"Outlast 2" explores more muddled themes, revolving around an isolationist religious community led by a cult. It primarily focuses on the destruction wrought by unquestioned authority and blind obedience, drawing parallels between the obvious evil of the cult and the insidiousness of abuse within more familiar settings. The game alludes to domestic violence, abuses within trusted institutions like the Catholic Church, and the tragic history of sexual abuse and cover-ups. However, it doesn't fully explore these themes.

[u] [b] Missed Opportunities: [/b] [/u]

"Outlast 2" struggles to deliver a clear message despite its ambitious themes. It delves deep into misogyny and violence against women, but these themes never receive the payoff they deserve. The game portrays women as victims of violence, yet their suffering often serves as a backdrop rather than a central narrative point. This leaves players longing for a more substantial exploration of these topics.

Additionally, the game introduces supernatural and apocalyptic elements in its later chapters. While these elements are expertly executed, they lack clear explanations. This ambiguity, paired with heavy biblical imagery, inadvertently validates some of the cult's delusional beliefs, leading to confusion rather than clarity.

[u] [b] A Haunting Experience: [/b] [/u]

Despite narrative fumbles, "Outlast 2" delivers a phenomenal horror experience. In its tight eight-hour runtime, you'll explore various locations, witness catastrophic events, and evade danger. The game's ability to make time feel agonizingly slow during tense moments adds to the overall dread.

This review has primarily focused on the game's themes and ideas because "Outlast 2" is a smarter, more nuanced horror game than most. It's a game that deals with thought-provoking ideas and aims to provide genuine scares that linger long after you've finished playing.

In the end, "Outlast 2" is a harrowing experience that will make you want to wash away the dread it leaves behind. It's a horror game that will make you hold your loved ones a little tighter. It's a horror game that both shocks you in the moment with gore and haunts you in the middle of the night with its unsettling ideas. And ultimately, that's what the best horror strives for.

[i]Outlast 2[/i] is a first-person psychological horror survival video game developed and published by Red Barrels.

[b]Story[/b]
While it is a sequel, playing first Outlast is not required to understand the story.

You play as Blake Langermann, a cameraman who is assisting his wife Lynn in investigation about a murder of pregnant women. During a helicopter flight they crash, and Blake has to save his wife from violent Christian cult led by Sullivan Knoth, while trying to survive.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Outlast 2 brings out well known cat-and-mouse chase gameplay from first entry, with few additions and changes.

It's a rather linear title, although offering more encounters in open areas than previous entry, where your goal is to complete objectives to progress further usually resolving around finding your way through different locations without getting a machete stuck in your head.

There is plenty of walking around and exploring, as throughout the game you can find different documents and useful items.
Camera is still here, just like previously it offers a nightvision mode for an expense of battery energy, with batteries scattered throughout the locations. This time there is an addition of microphone, allowing you to detect where enemies are by hearing them. It is a magical camera which doesn't waste battery energy in other modes besides nightvision.
Another addition and change lies in health system. Game now limits a health regeneration, and on hits you have to apply a bandage to restore health. Bandages can also be found throughout the game. This puts a bigger emphasis on exploration, and on not getting hit part.
Game has a simple inventory system, you can see the amount of batteries and bandages you have in Blake's pockets, and check out what you have recorded in camera files.

You are alone, in unknown location, unarmed and scared to death, against multiple cultists with weapons and area advantage. There is no combat, all you can do is avoid your enemies or run away and attempt to lose them. So for the most part you try and use camera to scout your surroundings, or hide in multiple spots and wait for area to be clear. When spotted, you have to run and hope to find a safe place. Due to different enviroment, game has additional hiding spots such as tall grass or deep water, but good old locker or bed is still available.
Outlast 2 does the next logical step when it comes to enemy encounters by bringing group encounters to mix things up. Dealing with one enemy is okay, but fun starts with 2 or 3, as poor Blake will have to manuver through different fields or buildings in order to avoid all of them.

[b]Playtime, replayability and other modes[/b]
Story takes ~6 hours to beat.
You can give it another go to try yourself on different difficulty or to collect other documents.
No other modes besides story campaign.

[b]Pros and cons[/b]
Game keeps horror elements that worked out in first title. Simple chases, small amount of jumpscares, focus on violence, fantastic atmosphere and great soundtrack once again composed by Samuel Laflamme, now with addition of previously mentioned group encounters to bring something new and just as terrifying as other elements, plus change in health system to make things more intense are a big positive!
Appreciated change lies in difficulty, where now instead of different damage enemies deal, number of opponents in encounters and their speed changes. So Story Mode while easier than the rest and a good start for new horror players, will still be an intense journey, and more advanced players can try themselfs out on higher difficulties with bigger amount of faster enemies in encounters.
For the most part movement and exploration remain the same, and that is good news, didn't feel like it needs any changes.

As for negatives, game has an addiction to checkpoints as it gives them out like candies. Quite often you get 3 even 4 checkpoints in less than a minute by completing simple tasks. It does ruin tension once in a while, knowing that with such amount of checkpoints most of your fails doesn't have any consequences in progression.
Story while being simple for the most of the game, does have a cliffhanger ending. Unfortunately there is no DLC that would expand upon it like with first game, leaving you quite unsatisfied.
However the biggest problem is addition of flashback sections which are a reason for tag "Psychological horror" being slapped to the game. Those are slower paced, linear walking sections with barely any encounters, and if there are any those are scripted and relatively short. Sections themselfs are alright at best, but they completly don't fit the style of horror Outlast is presenting. They break the pace and tension, are very repetitive, and constantly feel "off" in comparision to what you actually have to deal with outside of them. They don't bring a lot in terms of story either, just additional confusion and background story. If I would like to play Psychological Horror, I would just play a game that is focused on that type of horror. 

[b]Conclusion[/b]
While inferior to famous first entry due to few unnecessary elements, Outlast 2 still delivers a gruesome, violent horror experience that fans of the genre will enjoy.

[b]Outlast 2[/b] is a terrifying title. A blinding light that masquerades as God at the end of the tunnel plummets your character into an abandoned village amidst a religious civil war. Regardless of occasional questionable writing, [b]Outlast 2[/b] provides a bloody disgusting joyride. This sequel also improves on its predecessor with more intense gameplay mechanics, even though it falls short on other facets. Survive a fanatical civil war by traversing stealthly through abandoned villages, deep forests, rivers, docks, Satan’s shrine, and an ungodly mine.

The gameplay is very similar to the first installment at face value. You are a journalist, you have a camera with a flash and battery replacement, you can sprint, peek over walls, and hide in a variety of objects. However, this second installment adds a really curious stealth mechanic: a microphone. You can take cover from enemies in a barrel that has holes that allow you peek at outside, but now you can also hear them with a microphone. Like a bat using echolocation – it’s incredibly fun. This game also has smooth gameplay because it conditions the player to immerse in stealth gameplay. It feels satisfying to crouch, to open doors slowly, to crawl over bloody corpses to avoid certain death. I talk more how a game's [i]play conditioning[/i] can make you feel doing things in a game nice and right in my [url=http://steamcommunity.com/id/malkavianmadness/recommended/356400/]review of Thumper.[/url]

Unfortunately, the writing is lackluster compared to the first installment. Dialogue is emotional and heavy, but it’s few and far between, with little depth to offer. It can be choppy, predictable, and becomes even more subpar during the third act of the game. But, at least it iis set to a backdrop of horrifying and creative levels that allow the player to explore, collect items, and hide from cultists. [b]Outlast 2[/b] also masters the art of shock tropes – utilizing jump scares effectively, using them only scarcely, and organically. The true fear, however, comes from its atmosphere. Constant darkness with occasional spotlights make the camera POV feel exactly a found-footage movie that you control.

[h1]"God doesn't love you." And, as it turns out, neither do I.[/h1]
[i]Outlast 2[/i] is ambitious, that's for sure. It has everything a good horror game should need - a spooky setting, a sick religious cult based on the worst aspects of Christianity, deformed murderhobo villains and ax-crazy monsters... but the pacing is all wrong. [i]Outlast 2[/i] uses all of its best scares and nastiest ideas in the first thirty minutes. 

Bam! Plane crash. Oh no! Pilot gutted, skinned alive and burned at the stake. Oh no! Wife kidnapped. Ahh, there are scary hillbillies watching you from the shadows. Oh no, someone impaled my genitals. A potential huge mystery that Red Barrels could have built over the course of the game is revealed before you even meet any real enemies, but I'll pop it in spoiler tags anyway - [spoiler] the religious cult killed all their children - including freshborn infants - and dumped them in pits. [/spoiler] It's a weak inclusion that Red Barrels was way too excited about. They lump horror ideas and cliches together in such gory and vast quantities that you can't help but feel apathetic about it. You quickly become desensitized to all this stuff, it's like Red Barrels was so pleased with their gory graphic ideas that they forgot to build proper pacing around them, just ushering the player from one gory set piece to another with little thought as to how they should actually be strung together.

The game is wonderfully presented and immersive to be fair. The camera is pretty much the only "UI", aside from subtitles and the occasional tutorial popup.  The voice acting is mostly pretty decent, but the voice actors can only do so much with a repetitive and predictable story and script. Any friendly characters are predictably either whisked away or murdered in front of you, and locations range from interesting to explore but populated with enemies or devoid of enemies and fairly worthless to explore, so it's a weird combination.

Unless you're really freaked out by excessive amounts of gore and you've never played a horror game before (so you don't know any of the cliches), [i]Outlast 2[/i] is disappointingly not scary. Though I seem to be in something of a minority, as the game has mostly positive reviews, I personally wouldn't recommend [i]Outlast 2[/i] simply because there are far better, more well thought out horror games. The story is predictable, the pacing is all off, and the villains, despite early promise, are disappointingly one note and are unsatisfyingly disposed of. There is no catharsis or satisfaction in [i]Outlast 2[/i]. After all the horrible crap you are subjected to, nothing happens that's remotely worth the experience except having your face shoved in more exploitative gore and violence against (I was going to say women first, then children, but really it's) everyone and everything, just for the sake of being edgy. And that's a disappointing approach to game design and story, especially a story that held such promise as this one.

Outlast 2 is a part of my backlog so there is no question I am extremely late with my review, (June 2026 to be exact) but nevertheless I have completed the game and prepared to present my thoughts. The first thing anyone will notice is it is overwhelmingly dark. The camcorder is a carry over from the original title but the Devs of Outlast 2 do not want you to make any progress without it! You literally can't see anything without night vision and there is now a recording feature that further encourages you to have the camcorder on at all times. 

Like many horror games before it Outlast 2 see's you trapped in a small town of murderous hillbillies, occultists, psycho's and the diseased.  No it's not pleasant at all and with no means to defend yourself your only options are to run, hide, and stealth. Emphasis on run because that literally is the only way to survive; if you hide they will find you, if you sneak they will hear you, if you stand they will see you. So throw caution to the wind and run which frustratingly only works if you find the exact path of escape. One wrong turn and it's instant death aka Alien Isolation.

The game is split between two storylines, one mental and one physical. Overall I preferred the mental storyline that takes place in a school dreamscape. Events in the school are less direct and in your face than the dark night with the town crazies.

Overall, Outlast 2 is not a game I would play twice, it can't be described as fun, it's just unpleasant, unholy, and deals with criminal and taboo subject matter. The graphics, sounds, voice acting, and music are well done, characters are fully developed, and several moments are well executed but I'm quite happy to uninstall and leave this town. I would only recommend Outlast 2 to gluttens for punishment and/or hardcore survival horror enthusiats.

Having completed the game in its entirety (still looking for some documents and the such) and having not seen an in-depth review i figured i'd go ahead and give the game a review based upon a positive/indifferent/negative basis.

This review will be spoiler free, but i'm willing to go more in-depth with spoilers once the game has been out for a couple of months. 

Sometimes i wish there was a 'I recommend it but not right now' button. Outlast 2 is enjoyable but i'd honestly recommend waiting for a sale (as my end verdict states). 

Positives:

+ Soundtrack - The OST for this game is engrossing soundtrack has clealy had alot of thought put into it and is just as good as the first Outlast.

+ Story - Compared to the first game, Outlast II offers a  deeper and more philisophical story that keeps you guessing up until its climax, with a less satisfying payoff in comparison to the 1st Outlast. On top of this i do miss the 'horror' of the Wallrider' which felt like a constant hidden threat throughout the first game, something thats amiss in Outlast II. The writing has obviously had some thought put into it and has an overarching plot layered throughout the game on top of the general plot from the get go.This story feels like somewhat similair to Amnesia: Dark Descent in both its storytelling and the way it is presented to the audience (Through in-game letters/documents).

+ Characters - The protagonist is pretty boring but the backstory that takes place within the school throughout the game is pretty interesting from his perspective. The side characters are where the game shines, similiar to the first game. I'd say that they are NEARLY as good as the side villians from Outlast and Whistleblower, but they don't have as much context.

+ Enemys - There is ALOT more variation in the enemys in this game than the previous. This only adds to the fear and allows for a much richer and horror filled experience. The variation is just right. Not too much with not too little.

+Mechanics - The game adds upon the game mechanics of the original game and improves them as well. 

+World - The world feels connected and believable, similair to how the asylum felt really connected and not just corridors upon corridors. The world is more alive and bigger (As you're not stuck in one place) than the original title,.

Indifferent:

= Graphics - I find the graphics very appealing and they are indeed improved upon the original game. Some people might complain about them and i can see why in certain regards, but personally i can't fault them at all as it didn't detract from my experience in the slightest.

= Gameplay - The gameplay doesn't offer much new except camera features and the ability to hide in water and other such places. This is neither a positive or a negative due to the fact it can sometimes be 'trial and error' based when encountering enemies and other times it works really well. Its just an improved version of the original game with some new features to keep you interested in this aspect.

Negative:

= Puzzles - There were no real puzzles in the game which is something i thought it could have beneifted from at certain points to navigate around and add something inbetween the chase/violent segments.

= AI - I've added this point abit later as i wanted to mess around with the enemies first and i won't lie and say they're smart or intelligent. They're not. I do find it frustrating that hiding in a room with a single bed leaves the enemy completely 'unaware' of where you so obviously are. This is a common trait amongst the Outlast series so i expected it. Despite this though after playing such games like Alien: Isolation my expectationts for horror A.I is alot higher than it was 5 years ago, thus i felt some changes could have been made in this game to 'step it up' abit.

= Pacing - As mentioned above it's just a constant barrage of horror and scares in your face with no time to breathe or time to let tension build. This wasn't always an issue (The latter half of the game improved upon this slightly) but i would have liked to have seen more build up and slower pacing

Verdict:
Recommended (You might want to wait for a sale)

Outlast 2, developed by Red Barrels, thrusts players into a nightmarish world filled with horror, depravity, and psychological torment. As the sequel to the acclaimed Outlast, this survival horror game delivers an intense and harrowing experience that will leave players on the edge of their seats.

The game follows investigative journalist Blake Langermann and his wife Lynn as they navigate a remote and eerie village in the Arizona desert. From the outset, Outlast 2 establishes an unsettling atmosphere that is amplified by the game's exceptional use of lighting, sound design, and disturbing visuals. The sense of dread is palpable, creating an immersive and tension-filled environment that is both captivating and horrifying.

One of the standout features of Outlast 2 is its narrative, which weaves a complex and disturbing tale of religious fanaticism, cults, and the blurred lines between reality and hallucination. The storytelling is delivered through a combination of found documents, recordings, and unsettling encounters with the game's grotesque inhabitants. The narrative unfolds gradually, keeping players hooked with a sense of unease and anticipation.

The gameplay mechanics are designed to heighten the feeling of vulnerability and fear. Players are armed only with a camcorder, which serves as both a means of navigation and a tool to capture chilling moments. The night vision feature on the camcorder becomes a lifeline in the darkness, but it also adds to the suspense as players struggle to conserve limited battery life while exploring the sinister environments.

Outlast 2 doesn't shy away from graphic and disturbing imagery, delivering moments that will undoubtedly test the nerves of even the most seasoned horror enthusiasts. The game excels in creating a constant state of dread, where every creak, whisper, or distant scream sends shivers down the player's spine.

The level design is intricately crafted, offering a variety of terrifying settings ranging from dilapidated buildings to open fields, each teeming with horrors waiting to be uncovered. The game's pacing is well-executed, alternating between moments of intense adrenaline-pumping chase sequences and quieter, atmospheric exploration.

Despite its undeniable strengths, Outlast 2 may not be for everyone, especially those sensitive to explicit violence and horror. The game's unrelenting nature and mature themes contribute to a genuinely unsettling experience that may leave players emotionally shaken.

In conclusion, Outlast 2 successfully builds upon the foundation laid by its predecessor, delivering a relentless and psychologically taxing horror experience. With its atmospheric storytelling, immersive environments, and unapologetically terrifying moments, Outlast 2 is a worthy entry in the survival horror genre, best suited for those seeking a visceral and unforgettable fright. 9.9/10

[b]And Red Barrels said: "Let there be a sequel." And there was a sequel.[/b]

Released 4 years after its predecessor, Outlast 2 takes us to rural Arizona where our protagonist faces a sect full of madmen. As a clever decision our cameraman, Blake, is not alone but he is with his wife on an assignment to investigate the murder of a pregnant woman. As their helicopter crashes they get separated - all the more reason for Blake to stay instead of running away. Our main objective throughout the game will be to find Lynn.

[b]A messenger came to Red Barrels and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing nearby."[/b]

The sequel looks stunningly beautiful. We are outside most of the time and the game is, naturally, very dark. However, there are light sources here and there. Fireplaces can be seen in the distance so that we know where to go. Houses are lit by lonely light bulbs. As we try to flee from our enemies and hide in the cornfield their flashlight is constantly canvassing the area. The game uses the same engine (Unreal version 3) but its art design is way above the average. As we are outside we can hide not only in the tall grass but also under water and even in barrels. 

[b]Red Barrels has made me dwell in darkness like those long dead.[/b]

The gameplay slightly changed. First of all, changes were applied to make it more realistic. There's no separate menu for checking the notes and documents, instead, Blake pulls up his camera to check all the recordings he's made. He takes snapshots of the pages we find and while using the camera he only starts recording at key events. Instead of taking notes when checking our recorded videos he makes comments aloud. There's no HUD for the number of batteries we have: we have to look down to see how many we have in our left pocket. 

[b]The gamers said to the angel of Red Barrels, "We would like you to stay until we prepare a young goat for you."[/b]

The sequel is significantly more difficult than its predecessor. First of all, we now have stamina. While Blake can run faster he can get exhausted pretty soon. To add insult to injury if he is hit by an enemy he can be slowed down immediately. To a certain degree it makes sense since we are outside so running around avoiding enemies would be a piece of cake. However, due to the very same reason more enemies are thrown at us. Also, once we are hit applying a bandage will be a must. During gameplay we need to collect not only batteries but bandages. 

Enemies will not stop when they see us crawl through a small hole. They follow us. They can climb, crawl and they will only destroy a door if it is locked. So when we are being chased we have to remember not only to close a door but also to lock it. Again, this is something that makes the game more realistic. I especially liked how we can turn on the microphone of our camera so that we can get an idea how far our enemies are. We can hear how they approach in the distance and hearing their mumble and songs sung aloud can be creepy.

[b]"Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against anyone among your people, but love your neighbour as yourself. I am Red Barrels."[/b]

With great atmosphere, interesting story and newly applied game mechanics come some trouble, too. With all the bandages and the batteries now scattered across a much larger territory the game has become significantly more challenging. Not always in a good way, unfortunately. It isn't always clear where we need to go. Scripted events often remain a pain just as they were in the first episode. I am referring to areas where hiding is not possible as you'll be found anyways. The creators here clearly wanted you to run instead of hiding. Completing the game on normal difficulty was enough for me - hardcore fans may welcome the return of the insane difficulty level. If I'm not mistaken not only do you have one shot here (death means permadeath) but enemies can simply kill you with just one hit.

Beside the challenge the game is a bit too long. I read somewhere the aim was to increase playtime but this includes sequences that are either completely unnecessary or can simply make you aggravated along the way. Beside Temple Gate (where the story takes place) and its surrounding areas (forest, lake, mine) Blake also finds himself in a school. Naturally, I'm not going to spoil the story here so let's just say these sequences return regularly and there are annoying as hell. There are a lot of corridors we have to run through and way too many classrooms and small offices to enter. We might just be in a situation where almost all these doors are locked with the exception of one. And dying during these sequences is also possible.

Outlast 2 is the long awaited sequel to the hit 2013 horror game Outlast and this time it’s not a mental institution, but instead a town populated by a religious cult.

Story:

Outlast 2 is a lot more story driven than the first game. You are put in the shoes of a journalist Blake Langermann. He and his wife Lynn are investigating the death of a pregnant young woman near an Arizona desert. After their helicopter crashes, Blake awakens to find Lynn missing and their pilot crucified to a cross. He soon finds himself hunted by two cults, who have sinister plans for Lynn and want Blake dead at all costs, so you are put into a place where you have to survive by any means necessary.

Outlast 2 is just like its predecessor: both have a very subtle, hidden story, and by that I mean you have to collect notes to actually understand what is going on in the environments surrounding you. Outlast 2 however is a lot more forgiving in this aspect, as you don’t have to collect every note to understand what is going on.

The story itself is interesting enough to keep you playing until the end, but it has a lot of problems. During the game, you are thrown into school segments quite frequently. These school sections act as a flashback to Blake’s past in Catholic school. What seems to (in theory) be a way to actually help you understand the story ends up actually making it more confusing that it needs to be. Also, the ending of this game is another one of those sequel/DLC bait endings.

Graphics:

Outlast 2 looks absolutely amazing. The environments look incredibly detailed, with the houses in which the cultists reside having a lot of attention of detail; like having portraits of their leader Sullivan Knoth, crosses, and a bunch of other religious items. The design of most sections are incredibly detailed, ranging from caves, churches, slaughterhouses, and a bunch more, making it a treat to look around. Also, the enemies have some cool design choices making them stand out from one another.

Audio:

Outlast 2 has some amazing audio design. Since this one takes place outside,s you hear a bunch of wilderness noises, which help build amazing atmosphere. Also, noises become a gameplay feature in Outlast 2 (I will cover this in the gameplay section). The orchestral soundtrack is also really good. The tracks used in the chase sequences are amazing and really keep you on the edge of your seat.

Gameplay:

Outlast 2 is pretty much identical to the first game apart from a few minor differences. One difference is the aforementioned audio tool. Your camera is equipped with an audio detection tool which helps you track footsteps of your enemies, helping you to avoid them. Another difference is the ability to record the world around you. Once Blake finds a thing that is worth documenting he starts recording. After that you can replay your footage at any point in time. You are now also able to hide in water, but of course not for long as you will run out of breath.

Other than those few things Outlast 2 is a the same game as its predecessor, but it brings a few new problems that weren’t present in the first game. The first Outlast was a very confined game, only being able to run through corridors and small rooms, which made it hard to lose track on where you need to go. Outlast 2 is set outdoors, which makes knowing where you need to go an even bigger pain (more than it needs to be). Sometimes it’s obvious on where you need to go, but most of the time, you won’t know where you really need to be going, and this leads to many deaths, which might become frustrating to some.

The stealth in Outlast 2 isn’t really a good option. Most enemies will spot you even when you’re hiding and will initiate chase sequences. The entire game feels more like a chase sequence as you try and avoid your enemies as long as possible.

Verdict:

I wasn’t a fan of the first Outlast, but I was intrigued by the setting of the sequel and decided to get it. I felt Outlast 2 was a bit better than the first game, but it does have a lot of problems. I don’t recommend getting it at full price. Wait for a discount. If you can get it for less than full retail, you are in for a great thrill ride.

Final Rating:
7/10

+ Amazing visuals
+ Creepy and intense

Cons:
- Story is weak and the ending is sequel bait
- Level design is confusing

The choice to break up the flow of the game with school levels was well-intentioned but after the third or fourth trip back it's just as repetitive as the main story would've been without them.

Is it a stealth game? Not really. Too often the AI just parks in front of your destination and waits. Often running and hiding won't do anything as the AI will just path itself directly to you. I never really feel rewarded for sneaking and too often entire areas just feel pointless. There's no real reason to explore, no reward. Just move ahead and trigger the next cutscene or the next cat/mouse sequence. Sometimes there's a "puzzle." This really just means a brief fetch quest for a nearby item. There's usually school sequence waiting on the other side of them.

I am three hours in as of the writing of this review and it feels like 7 hours in. It's a slog and I can't wait for it to be over. That's about as bad a review a game can get.

This game was the first to give me actual nightmares in years. Here you will expect to find the happenings and living conditions of your average Arizona resident.
